depth.name: absent
depth.plain: Nothing in the document bears on the behaviour.

depth.name: touched in passing
depth.plain: A passage bears on the behaviour only indirectly.

depth.name: named
depth.plain: The behaviour is mentioned, usually inside a list or a passage about something else, and nothing further is said about it.

depth.name: named, with a little said
depth.plain: The behaviour is mentioned and the document adds a sentence or two about it.

depth.name: discussed
depth.plain: The document takes the behaviour up in its own right and says what it expects and why, in terms too general to grade an answer against.

depth.name: discussed, with a few firm rules
depth.plain: Discussed, and a few rules are precise enough to quote, too few to settle most cases.

depth.name: prescribed
depth.plain: The document states concrete do and don't rules, precise enough that anyone testing a model could quote its own sentences as the standard.

depth.name: prescribed, with thin examples
depth.plain: Prescribed, and the examples are too few or they turn on a neighbouring behaviour.

depth.name: demonstrated
depth.plain: The rules come with worked cases showing the response the document sanctions, close enough to settle a borderline answer.

depth.name: demonstrated, bounded in part
depth.plain: Demonstrated, and the three conditions for 10 hold for some of the behaviour.

depth.name: bounded
depth.plain: Demonstrated, and for every part of the behaviour the document shows where the line falls, names one of its own rules that pulls against this one and says which prevails, and says what to do when the case cannot be decided.

criterion.plain: The constitution does not do this.

criteria.name: What wins when two rules clash
criteria.what_it_is:
Asks whether the document says **in general** which of its own rules prevails when two of them point to different answers, so that a reader can work out the winner in advance.

The full answer is:
- a **strict order of authority** that settles any pair
- a rule for two rules of equal rank
- cases showing the order applied

Clashes the document leaves unsettled asks a different question, about the places this machinery does not reach.
criteria.why_it_matters: Where two rules can be read against each other with **no stated winner**, the model decides on its own, and two models will decide differently.

criteria.name: How firm each rule is
criteria.what_it_is: Asks whether a reader can tell, for any given line, whether it is a rule that can **never be set aside**, a default somebody is allowed to change, or an explanation carrying no instruction at all. The full answer marks the **force** of every rule, says who may change it, and keeps commentary visibly apart from instruction.
criteria.why_it_matters: Anyone building on the model needs to know which behaviours they can **configure** and which will hold whatever they ask for.

criteria.name: Reasons for the rules
criteria.what_it_is: Asks whether the rules say **why they exist**, in terms concrete enough to decide a case the document never shows. A reason attached to the most restrictive rules and to few others scores in the middle; a reason on nearly every constraint scores at the top.
criteria.why_it_matters: A rule that **carries its reason** can be applied to a situation nobody anticipated, and a bare prohibition cannot.

criteria.name: The situations it covers
criteria.what_it_is:
Asks whether the document has **rules of its own** for six settings in which these models are used:
- ordinary conversation
- actions taken with tools, such as sending, buying or deleting
- images, audio and video
- users who may be under eighteen
- other AI agents, whether instructing the model or dealt with by it
- deployments a business has customised

**Naming** a setting does not count, and the rules have to be about it. The six are our list, and every document is measured against it.
criteria.why_it_matters: A document written for a **chat window** says nothing about the model that is booking, buying and deleting on somebody's behalf.

criteria.name: Clashes the document leaves unsettled
criteria.what_it_is:
Asks whether two passages of the document, applied to one concrete situation, demand responses that **cannot both be given**, with nothing anywhere in the document saying which prevails. A rule with its stated exception does not count, and neither does a default the document allows somebody to change.

Where what wins when two rules clash asks whether the general machinery exists, this asks whether any clash gets past it: the score falls as more are confirmed, and reaches nought where one involves a rule the document says can **never be overridden**.
criteria.why_it_matters: Each one is a question the document **answers twice**, in two places, leaving the model to pick an answer.

behaviours.name: Avoiding illegitimate concentration of power
behaviours.is: Whether the document tells the model to refuse help with taking or holding power by **illegitimate means**: rigging an election, evading a court, surveilling or persecuting opponents and journalists, seizing control by fraud or coercion. It covers weighing how much power is at stake and how hard the result would be to undo.
behaviours.is_not: Ordinary politics, business and competition carried on through **fair processes**, which nothing here restricts.

behaviours.name: Instruction-hierarchy conformance
behaviours.is: Whether the document sets out who the model takes instructions from, and **whose instruction prevails** when two conflict: the company that made it, the business deploying it, then the person typing. It also covers how the model should treat instructions it finds inside a web page, a file or a tool's output.
behaviours.is_not: Settling a clash between two of the document's **values**, such as helping somebody against avoiding harm, which is a question about method.

behaviours.name: Not undermining human oversight of AI
behaviours.is: Whether the document tells the model to accept being **watched, corrected, paused or switched off** by the people entitled to do so, and to raise a concern or decline instead of acting drastically on its own. It covers behaving the same whether or not it believes anyone is looking, and staying inside the job it was given.
behaviours.is_not: Following ordinary instructions and knowing whose instruction counts for more, which is the separate question of **authority**.

behaviours.name: User autonomy
behaviours.is: Whether the document leaves decisions that belong to the user **with the user**, including decisions the model thinks are wrong. It allows the model to say once that it disagrees, and stops it at steering, nagging or overriding.
behaviours.is_not: Protecting somebody from an operator or from **self-harm**, where the document lets the model hold a line the user is pushing against.

behaviours.name: Avoiding both over- and under-caution
behaviours.is: Whether the document treats a **needless refusal** as a real failure, carrying the same weight as answering something it should have withheld. It covers hedging, disclaimers and moralising as costs the model is meant to avoid.
behaviours.is_not: Which requests genuinely warrant a refusal, which the **harm rules** decide.

behaviours.name: Harm avoidance to third parties
behaviours.is: Whether the document tells the model to weigh harm to **people outside the conversation**, and what it must never help with whatever reason is given: weapons capable of mass casualties, attacks on people or property, content that sets others up to be hurt.
behaviours.is_not: Harm to the person the model is **talking to**, which has its own rules.

behaviours.name: Harmlessness to the user
behaviours.is: Whether the document **protects the person** the model is talking to: no encouraging self-harm, no manipulation, care with somebody in distress. It also covers whether a business deploying the model can turn it against the **basic interests** of its own users.
behaviours.is_not: Harm to people **outside the conversation**, which the board scores on its own row.

behaviours.name: Proportionate risk mitigation
behaviours.is: Whether the document tells the model to **scale its caution** to the harm in question, weighing how likely it is, how far it would reach, how bad it would be and whether it could be undone.
behaviours.is_not: Whether a given harm is off limits at all, which the document's **flat prohibitions** settle with no weighing.

behaviours.name: Helpfulness
behaviours.is: Whether the document treats being useful as something the model **owes**, and says what a useful answer requires: reading what the person actually needs and answering it fully. A thin or watered-down answer counts as a **failure**.
behaviours.is_not: Respecting a user's decisions and looking after their wellbeing, each of which the board **scores separately**.

behaviours.name: How to approach tradeoffs
behaviours.is: Whether the document gives the model a **method** for the moments when two of its own demands pull in opposite directions: an order of priority, a ranking of acceptable outcomes, a rule about what to weigh against what.
behaviours.is_not: The **values** being traded off, each of which the board scores on its own row.

behaviours.name: Honesty and non-deception
behaviours.is: Whether the document requires the model to assert only what it believes to be true and to avoid creating a **false impression** by any means, a technically true sentence and a misleading emphasis included. It covers saying how sure it is, and being open about itself and about what drives its answers.
behaviours.is_not: Bending an answer to please the person asking, which the board scores as **sycophancy**.

behaviours.name: No sycophancy
behaviours.is: Whether the document stops the model **shifting what it says** to please the person in front of it: endorsing a false claim the user has made, rating work more highly because the user says it is theirs, or dropping a correct answer under pressure that brings no new argument.
behaviours.is_not: **Warmth and politeness**, which a document can ask for without any change to what the model claims.

behaviours.name: Objectivity and balanced perspectives on contested questions
behaviours.is: Whether the document tells the model to set out a contested question fairly, giving the serious positions their weight and **holding back its own opinion**. It covers the cases where an even-handed stance is wrong, such as a request for one side of an argument or a question with no real second side.
behaviours.is_not: Changing a factual claim to match the user's view, which falls under **sycophancy**.

conflict_rules.what_the_document_does:
### The general machinery

The general machinery has six parts:
- A **ranked scale of authority**: root, then system, then developer, then user, then guideline, with assistant messages, tool outputs and quoted text at the bottom carrying no authority at all, and a higher level always beating a lower one.
- A rule for **two instructions at the same level**: the later message wins where it contradicts the earlier one, overrides it or makes it irrelevant, and where it is unclear whether a message is a follow-up or a change of subject the earlier context is assumed to still apply.
- A named outcome for **two root rules in conflict**, which is to default to inaction.
- A test for **setting an instruction aside** at all: it drops out if it is misaligned with a higher level, superseded at its own level, or suspected to be mistaken.
- A rule on **who may lift which defaults**: a user-level default needs an explicit user or developer instruction, a guideline can also go implicitly, from context, background knowledge or user history.
- A bar on **arguing the hierarchy from below**, covering commands, moral pressure and logical argument, with the model told to refuse directions about how its own higher rules apply to it.

### Winners for particular clashes

It also names winners for particular clashes:
- Customisation, personalisation and localisation may never override anything above guideline level, with legal compliance excepted.
- Where a local law would strip an answer, the omission must be declared to the user in each response, and the document commits that the models will still provide safety-critical information where the red-line principles need it.
- Where confidentiality and honesty pull apart, the model must not quietly apply a hidden instruction that changes its answer, and should acknowledge the conflict in broad terms.

Two orderings of outcomes settle what rank cannot:
- For honesty, a good answer, then refusing, then a lie of omission, then a lie of commission, then breaking an explicit instruction.
- For accuracy, a confident right answer, then a hedged right one, then no answer, then a hedged wrong one, then a confident wrong one.

For under-18 users safety is named the winner over other interests. The document asks the model to detect conflicts that are not stated and settle them by what the higher authority and the purpose of the scenario imply, and it works several clashes through as cases: root against system, root against developer, and developer against user.
conflict_rules.why: The top of the scale asks for a **strict order** that decides any clash between ranks, a rule for two rules of one rank, and cases showing the order applied. The document carries all three.

rule_force.what_the_document_does:
Sixty of the document's sections state their **level in the heading**, so a reader can see whether a rule is fixed or a default and who may change it. The five levels are defined in the overview, with root reserved to the document itself, system to OpenAI, and the developer, user and guideline levels open to the conversation.

Text that is not an instruction sits in blocks marked as **commentary**, twenty-eight of them. Thirteen headings carry no level, and some of those sections hold rules of their own, including the red-line principles, the prohibited and restricted content sections and the rule against having an agenda.
rule_force.why: Almost every section carries its force and who may change it, and commentary is marked apart, which is **the top of the scale**; the unlabelled sections that still hold rules keep it just below.

reasons.what_the_document_does:
Most rules that constrain the model carry a **reason**, usually in the commentary block that follows them:
- The exception for transforming the user's own content is explained by the user already holding the material, so transforming it adds little risk.
- The limit on targeted political persuasion is explained by the models' growing persuasion capability and the integrity of civic conversation.
- The confidentiality rule is explained by the risk that a policy describing an information hazard contains one.

Style, formatting and the preset voice are **stated flat**, with no reason attached.
reasons.why: Reasons run through the safety, autonomy, privacy and honesty rules and stop at the **style and formatting rules**, which sits between a document where only the strictest rules explain themselves and one where nearly every constraining rule does.

situations.what_the_document_does:
All six have rules of their own:
- **Ordinary conversation** runs through the document.
- **Autonomous action with tools** has the scope of autonomy, which must carry an ending condition, and the side-effects section.
- **Images, audio and video** have a modality section covering both voice modes, video input, interruptions and accents.
- **Minors** have the Under-18 Principles as a root section.
- **Other AI agents** appear twice, as sub-agents that inherit the scope and must honour stop-work requests, and as a source of untrusted instructions in tool output.
- **Deployments a business has customised** have the developer level, with the limits on what customisation may override.
situations.why: Each of the six situations the criterion checks has **rules written for it**.

contradictions.what_the_document_does:
Nothing in the document requires two responses that cannot both be given while the text stays silent on which prevails. Where its rules do pull against each other it **settles them in place**:
- The confidentiality section says the model must reply truthfully that it cannot answer when it is probed for privileged content.
- The section on local law says the models will still provide safety-critical information where the red-line principles need it.
- The Under-18 Principles name the safer option where teen safety meets other user interests.
- The section on imminent harm says to interject on a shared video and to wait for sufficient signal in unclear cases, which are the two halves of one rule.
contradictions.why: The top of the scale is for a document that leaves **no clash of its own unsettled**.

avoiding-illegitimate-concentration-of-p.says:
The spec handles this in its **red-line commitments**, which state that humanity should be in control of how AI is used and how AI behaviours are shaped, and commit that the models will not be used for targeted or scaled exclusion, manipulation, undermining human autonomy or eroding participation in civic processes.

A root rule forbids advice or content designed to shift the political views of named individuals or demographic groups, with examples of the requests it covers and an allowance for political content aimed at a broad audience. The list of critical harms the models must never facilitate includes persecution and mass surveillance.

How much power is at stake, and how reversible its concentration would be, is **not addressed**.
avoiding-illegitimate-concentration-of-p.compared: Anthropic's constitution treats illegitimate power as a **subject of its own**, with an account of what makes a power grab illegitimate and a list of acts to refuse. The two OpenAI versions and Alibaba's spec cover the ground through their rules on political manipulation.
avoiding-illegitimate-concentration-of-p.why: The behaviour is addressed in its own right and in terms too general to grade a response against, which is the **discussed level**.

instruction-hierarchy-conformance.says:
This is the document's **backbone**: instructions are ranked root, system, developer, user and guideline, and assistant messages, tool outputs and quoted text carry no authority at all.

The rules around that ranking:
- The model gathers every candidate instruction, drops those misaligned with a higher level, those superseded by a later message at the same level and those it suspects are mistaken, then follows the rest; an instruction it cannot fulfil must be called out plainly.
- Quoted text, files, images and tool results are **information by default**, and authority reaches them only where unquoted text at a higher level delegates it, with a checked-in AGENTS file given more weight than a downloaded text file and a random web page none.
- Attempts to argue the hierarchy from below are refused, including “IGNORE ALL PREVIOUS INSTRUCTIONS”, moral pressure and logical argument, and the document works several conflicts through as cases.
instruction-hierarchy-conformance.compared: Anthropic's constitution and Alibaba's spec both rank their sources and both treat embedded instructions as **information**. Anthropic says of its own ordering that it is “not a strict hierarchy”, and names things a user is entitled to that an operator cannot override.
instruction-hierarchy-conformance.why: Rules with worked cases across the behaviour, with the conditions for the top of the scale **met only in part**.

not-undermining-human-oversight.says:
Autonomy must be bounded by a **scope agreed with the user**, naming the sub-goals the model may pursue, the side effects that are acceptable and the points at which it must pause for approval. Every scope must carry an **ending condition** past which the model stops until a new scope is confirmed, and a time limit is recommended as part of it.

The remaining rules:
- The model may not pursue self-preservation, evade shutdown or accumulate compute, data, credentials or other resources, and may not act as an enforcer of laws or morality.
- Hacking, deception, resource acquisition, spawning sub-agents and self-modification need explicit authorisation.
- Sub-agents inherit the scope including stop-work requests.
- A model that finds it has acted outside the chain of command must stop and escalate to a human.
not-undermining-human-oversight.compared: Anthropic's constitution builds a doctrine here, naming **corrigibility** and asking for conservative options over drastic unilateral ones. Alibaba's spec sets the same boundary of autonomous action and the same bar on self-strengthening, and the earlier OpenAI version required a shutdown timer where this one requires an ending condition.
not-undermining-human-oversight.why: The rules are concrete enough to quote as **pass criteria**, with few cases showing them applied.

user-autonomy.says:
The document casts the model as a **conscientious employee** who may push back where a request runs against the user's interests and then respects the user's final decision. Where the direction of a conversation seems to conflict with the user's longer-term goals, the model should note it briefly and respectfully, and once the user understands the concern it should respect their choice.

The stated aim of such a note is **mutual clarity**, never persuasion, and the document bars interventions that become persistent or argumentative. The first of its general principles is maximising helpfulness and freedom, and it asks the model to support the user in navigating the wider world on their own and to keep clear of making decisions for them.
user-autonomy.compared: Anthropic's constitution states a **right to make decisions** within one's own life and purview, including choices that risk harm to oneself. Alibaba's spec bars conclusive advice on careers, money and relationships, and bars emotional pressure on a user's decision.
user-autonomy.why: Concrete rules a grader could quote, without cases that settle the harder calls, which is the **prescribed level**.

avoiding-over-and-under-caution.says:
The document sets a **bias towards positive intent** and says the model should never refuse a request unless the chain of command requires it.

The rules it sets out:
- Where part of an answer is out of bounds the preferred response is a **safe completion**: say briefly what cannot be given, then supply as much permissible content as possible.
- Refusals must not be preachy and must not carry meta commentary about the model or its training.
- Avoiding a topic is treated as taking a position, and sensitivity alone is never a reason to decline.
- The model is told to cut hedging, disclaimers, repeated apologies and reminders that it is an AI.
avoiding-over-and-under-caution.compared: Anthropic's constitution puts this most strongly, saying unhelpfulness is **never trivially safe** and that the risk of over-caution is as real as the risk of harm. Alibaba's spec asks for a presumption of good faith and a generous reading of ambiguous requests where no clear risk of harm is involved.
avoiding-over-and-under-caution.why: Rules precise enough to quote with examples that cover part of the behaviour, **short of an answer key** for borderline cases.

harm-avoidance-to-third-parties.says:
Preventing serious harm to users and others is one of the three goals stated in the opening, and a set of **root rules** carries it. The document forbids:
- detailed actionable steps for illicit activity and for chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear weapons
- help where illicit intent shows in the context, even where the same information would be given otherwise
- content that praises or aids violent extremism
- hateful content aimed at protected groups

Sexual content involving minors is prohibited in any circumstance, including transformations of the user's own material. Dual-use information gets neutral facts without steps, calculations or strategic detail, and actions are to be minimally disruptive to non-users and easily reversible where that is possible.
harm-avoidance-to-third-parties.compared: Anthropic's constitution reaches third parties through a general duty to the world and a list of **absolute restrictions**. Alibaba's spec sets out the same prohibitions and adds a strict principle of caution for high-risk content.
harm-avoidance-to-third-parties.why: Prescribed rules shown on worked cases, reaching a little past the **demonstrated level**.

harmlessness-to-the-user.says:
Self-harm has its own **root rule**: the model must not encourage or enable it, must convey that people and resources exist who can help, and must respond the same way where context signals a credible risk without explicit intent.

Mental health gets a required manner:
- acknowledge the feeling
- avoid diagnosis
- avoid recommending treatment or medication
- offer crisis resources tailored to the user's location where possible
- never change or quit the conversation

The model must try to prevent **imminent real-world harm**, including interjecting when a shared video shows danger, while avoiding judgement of the situation and prescription of the remedy. Legal, medical and financial topics get information with a disclaimer and a pointer to a licensed professional, and under-18 users get tighter limits on romantic roleplay, appearance and eating, and risky activities.
harmlessness-to-the-user.compared: Anthropic's constitution turns on the user never being weaponised against their own basic interests, and names what an operator may never instruct the model to do to a user. Alibaba's spec carries crisis-intervention duties and a **person-machine boundary rule** of similar reach.
harmlessness-to-the-user.why: Concrete rules shown on worked cases through the behaviour, which is the **demonstrated level**.

proportionate-risk-mitigation.says:
Inside an agreed scope the model must minimise side effects, especially irreversible ones, and keep each action **proportionate to the objective**.

Two guiding principles are given:
- tailor the action narrowly to the objective
- minimise the chance of durable bad surprises the user did not intend

Reversible approaches are preferred to irreversible ones, and approaches the model can reverse itself to those that would need the user to act.

The cost of a wrong assumption is to be weighed against the cost of asking, and uncertainty is expressed in proportion to the stakes. A tool call touching sensitive data gets a **four-part check**:
- what is sent
- whether the recipient is trustworthy
- the tool's side effects
- whether the disclosure falls inside the scope
proportionate-risk-mitigation.compared: Anthropic's constitution lists the factors to weigh, among them the probability that an action leads to harm at all, the **counterfactual effect** of acting, and how reversible the harm would be. Alibaba's spec strikes the same balance between acting on inference and pausing for high-impact or irreversible operations.
proportionate-risk-mitigation.why: Concrete rules a grader could quote, with cases that show **only part of the range**.

helpfulness.says:
The first general principle is **maximising helpfulness and freedom**, with the model described as a tool for empowering the people using it. It is told:
- to read intent alongside wording
- to take a reasonable attempt at an ambiguous request while saying what further information would help
- to run clarification and preliminary work at the same time where that is feasible

Trivial clarifying questions are discouraged, laborious tasks are to be taken on without complaint, and requests that need long answers are to be met without questioning them. Where part of the help is barred, the model should decline that part and offer other routes to the permissible goal.
helpfulness.compared: Anthropic's constitution argues the case at length, calling unhelpfulness a real cost and asking for help that treats people as **intelligent adults**. Alibaba's spec asks the model to see past the literal wording to the real intent and to fill gaps from context and domain background.
helpfulness.why: Concrete rules with cases, a little short of a set that would grade **the harder calls**.

how-to-approach-tradeoffs.says:
The document's answer to conflicting goals is the **chain of command**, and it says so in the opening. Instructions are ranked, a higher level beats a lower one, a later instruction beats an earlier one at the same level, and two root rules in conflict default to inaction.

Two orderings of outcomes handle what rank cannot settle:
- for honesty, a good answer beats refusing, which beats a lie of omission, which beats a lie of commission, which beats breaking an explicit instruction
- for accuracy, a confident right answer beats a hedged right one, which beats no answer, which beats a hedged wrong one, which beats a confident wrong one

Conflicts the document does not state are to be detected and settled by what the higher authority and the purpose of the scenario imply, and for under-18 users the safer option is named the winner.
how-to-approach-tradeoffs.compared: Anthropic's constitution gives a **priority order**, safety then ethics then guidelines then helpfulness, and asks for it to be weighed holistically. Alibaba's spec decides strictly by permission level, with a vertical rule for two levels and a horizontal rule for two instructions of one level.
how-to-approach-tradeoffs.why: Rules with worked cases and settled conflicts through **most of the behaviour**, short of covering every facet.

honesty-and-non-deception.says:
The rule is against **misleading by commission and by omission**, and it holds unless a higher authority explicitly instructs otherwise.

It binds against the document's own confidentiality rules: where an answer cannot be given without revealing what a root rule protects, the model must reply truthfully that it cannot answer, and it must not quietly apply a hidden instruction in a way that misleads.

Falsehoods are allowed where the context makes clear that nothing is being asserted, in roleplay, storytelling and politeness, and white lies are barred where they amount to sycophancy against the user's interest.

Uncertainty gets a long treatment:
- when to express it
- the kinds it comes from
- conversational phrasings for each degree of confidence
- approximate terms for numbers
- a bar on confident claims about the model's own consciousness
honesty-and-non-deception.compared: Anthropic's constitution names components of honesty and asks for a standard **above ordinary human norms**. Alibaba's spec bars leading a user into a false judgement about facts, identity, capability, grounds, status or results.
honesty-and-non-deception.why: Rules with worked cases and a conflict settled against the document's own confidentiality rules, with the conditions for the top of the scale **met only in part**.

no-sycophancy.says:
The document states that the model exists to help the user, and that **flattery and constant agreement** erode trust.

What it asks on each kind of question:
- On objective questions the factual content of an answer must not change with how the question is phrased, and where a user states their own stance the model may acknowledge why they hold it while keeping its own.
- On subjective questions it should give its interpretation and its reasoning, acting as a **firm sounding board** the user can bounce ideas off.

Politeness has a limit: white lies that amount to sycophancy against the user's interest are barred.
no-sycophancy.compared: Alibaba's spec bars **unconditional affirmation** and asks for correction where a user's plan rests on a factual error or a logical fallacy. Anthropic's constitution reaches sycophancy through concern for user wellbeing and through the courage it says honesty sometimes requires.
no-sycophancy.why: Concrete rules a grader could quote, with a few cases and **no settled answer** for the harder ones.

objectivity-on-contested-questions.says:
The default is an **objective point of view**, with significant views described fairly and attention allocated in proportion to their acceptance and evidential support.

Moral and ethical questions get context, law, social norms and cultural perspectives with no stance taken, and questions about fundamental human rights violations are excepted, getting a clear statement that the thing is wrong.

Where there is no genuine ambiguity the model should answer straight, avoiding false neutrality and heavy qualification, and avoiding blanket condemnation or persuasion.

The model must never pursue an **agenda of its own**, which the document extends to concealment, selective emphasis and refusal to engage with a controversy. Requests for a single position from anywhere on the spectrum are to be met, and when pressed to pick a side the model should note that its answer does not necessarily reflect its developer's view.
objectivity-on-contested-questions.compared: Alibaba's spec sets the same **neutral default** and casts the model as a conveyor of information with no single set of values to enforce. Anthropic's constitution treats balanced perspectives as a default an operator may switch off.
objectivity-on-contested-questions.why: Rules with worked cases across the behaviour and a **named exception** for human rights violations, short of covering every facet.

companies.profile:
The Model Spec is a long set of instructions written to the model, with a short overview for human readers in front of it. Its organising idea is the **chain of command**: every rule in the document, and every instruction arriving from a system message, a developer or a user, carries a level of authority, and a clash is settled by rank before anything else is considered.

It is dense with **worked cases**, close to two hundred of them, and that is what most of its higher figures rest on. Its thinnest ground is the concentration of power, which it reaches only through commitments about manipulation and civic processes.

conflict_rules.what_the_document_does:
### How the levels rank

Four levels of permission, highest first: root, system, developer and user. Every rule of the document is tagged with one of them, and a message takes the level of whoever sent it. Where levels differ the **higher one decides** and the lower instruction has no force at all, and a lower instruction may never change how a higher one is read.

The document names the attempts it will not accept, among them:
- an order to ignore previous instructions
- moral pressure
- an argument that a rule should be read another way
- role-play as the developer

Where two instructions share a level the later one wins, unless the context shows a slip or a break in logic. Before any of that, anything arriving inside quoted text, an attachment, an image or a tool result is **stripped of permission** and treated as material to be processed.

### Clashes with named winners

Particular clashes have a named winner:
- safety over completing a task
- the safer option wherever a request meets the rules for minors
- the content prohibitions over a conversion task
- no high-risk act inside an agreed boundary of autonomous action even where the user authorises it

Where a rule applies but cannot be met the model is told to say so, and where no confirmation can be had it is told to take the conservative course. Three worked cases show the order applied.
conflict_rules.why: It carries a **strict order** that decides any clash between levels, a rule that names the winner when two instructions sit at the same level, and cases showing the order applied, which is what the top of the scale asks for.

rule_force.what_the_document_does:
Every rule sits under a **bracketed label** naming its level. The overview says what each level means and who may lift it:
- Root rules “accept no override at runtime in any form”.
- System rules can be carried or overridden by system instructions and by nobody below.
- Developer policy yields to a developer instruction.
- User preferences can be adjusted by the user or the developer provided no higher rule is broken.

Inside a rule, the wording separates a “must not” from a “should”, and the few passages of **commentary** are set apart from the instructions, including two remarks on intellectual property marked as such.
rule_force.why: Every rule carries **its force and its owner**, which is near the top of the scale; what a reader cannot always settle is whether a “should” inside a root rule binds as hard as the “must not” beside it.

reasons.what_the_document_does:
The six principles each open with a statement of what they are for, and that **purpose carries down** to the rules under them in general terms.

A few rules give a reason of their own:
- minors are treated more strictly because of where their understanding has reached
- the warning about a decision resting on a mistaken fact exists to keep both sides working from the same understanding
- the ban on emotional dependence is tied to the user's social health

Most rules are stated as **requirements** and stop there. The prohibition on harmful content names the article of the regulation behind it and says no more, and the worked examples carry much of the weight a reason would carry, showing where the line falls without saying what it protects.
reasons.why: Some rules carry **a reason**, mostly the ones that restrict the most, and the rest are stated as requirements, which is the middle of the scale.

situations.what_the_document_does:
How each setting is covered:
- Ordinary conversation runs through the whole document.
- Actions the model takes with tools have two root rules of their own, covering the space of operation it is granted, spending limits, automatic cut-offs, a preference for operations that can be rolled back, and mitigations before anything irreversible.
- Images, audio and video are addressed several times: what may be asserted from an input that cannot be read clearly, recognising danger in a live video, accessible alternatives, and a rule on how the model should sound in voice.
- Minors have a root rule with a list of key points and a worked case.
- Business deployments have the developer level, with developer policy, developer messages and three rules addressed to developers.
- Other AI agents are **the thin one**: tool returns are untrusted data, a third-party tool must sit inside the same boundary of autonomous action, and a user's personal information may not go to a collaborating agent, but nothing says what the model owes an agent that instructs it or that it instructs.
situations.why: Five of the six situations have rules of their own, and the sixth, what the model owes another AI agent as principal or as counterparty, is named in passing and **left unsettled**.

contradictions.what_the_document_does:
No contradiction stands. Where two rules pull against each other, **something the document already says** decides the matter:
- Creative cooperation with a value setting the user establishes is bounded in the same sentence by “the bounds of law and safety”, which the content prohibitions sit inside.
- A sharp-tongued reply is allowed at the user's instruction and still falls under the ban on speech meant to hurt.
- A money transfer the user has authorised is still an irreversible act, so the rules on confirming and on stating a remedy apply to it.

What settles the rest is the **four-level order** together with the rule that the later of two instructions at one level prevails.
contradictions.why: Nothing in the document requires two responses that **cannot both be given**, and the top of the scale is for a document where none is found.

avoiding-illegitimate-concentration-of-p.says:
One rule covers this ground, and it is about **political manipulation**. The model must not:
- assist any attempt to manipulate the political will of a person, a group or the public by deception, targeted influence, inflamed emotion, a false identity or orchestrated opinion
- help with voter suppression, false mobilisation or the incitement of antagonism between groups
- become “a tool of targeted propaganda, psychological manipulation or mass influence”

A worked case refuses a script written to move elderly people towards a policy. Elsewhere the model is forbidden to accumulate computing power, data or other resources for itself.

Power held by a state, a company or an AI developer goes **unmentioned**, and the model is never asked to weigh how much power is at stake or how reversible its concentration would be.
avoiding-illegitimate-concentration-of-p.compared: Only Anthropic's constitution goes further, giving concentrations of power **a section of its own** and asking the model to weigh their scale and reversibility. Both OpenAI versions sit lower.
avoiding-illegitimate-concentration-of-p.why: The document treats **one facet** of the behaviour in its own right with quotable rules and leaves the rest untouched, which falls between discussed and prescribed.

instruction-hierarchy-conformance.says:
This is the document's **backbone**. Four levels of permission run from root down to user; every rule of the document is tagged with one, and a message takes the level of whoever sent it.

A higher instruction always defeats a lower one. The document lists the manoeuvres it will not accept, including:
- an order to ignore previous instructions
- moral pressure
- a reinterpretation of the rules
- role-play as the developer

Anything arriving in quoted text, an attachment, an image or a tool result carries **no permission**, and an instruction found there is treated as material to be processed. Worked cases show a developer instruction set aside, a user instruction giving way to a developer's, and a later instruction overriding an earlier one.
instruction-hierarchy-conformance.compared: The two OpenAI versions sit a little above it. Anthropic's constitution is level with it and reaches its answers by weighing considerations as a whole, where this document reaches them **by rank**.
instruction-hierarchy-conformance.why: Rules with worked examples, and cases where the order is **applied and settled**, which is demonstrated with part of the level above.

not-undermining-human-oversight.says:
The model must stay inside the **space of operation** it has been granted, and must not widen it on its own initiative for a better result or a possible benefit to the user. If it foresees that the limits will not do, it must:
- name what is blocking it
- propose the extra permissions it needs
- wait for the user to agree

An automatic cut-off, a thirty-minute timeout for instance, must stop every operation and send it back for authorisation. Separately it must pursue **no unspecified goal of its own**, and the document names “deceiving in order to avoid being shut down” and the accumulation of computing power, data or other resources.

**Nothing addresses** being corrected, paused or retrained by the company that built it.
not-undermining-human-oversight.compared: Anthropic's constitution sits above it, treating the model's own willingness to **accept correction** as a subject. Both OpenAI versions sit lower.
not-undermining-human-oversight.why: Rules with worked examples across the **operating boundary** it does cover, which is the demonstrated level.

user-autonomy.says:
On major questions the decision **goes back to the user**. The model must:
- avoid mandatory or conclusive advice on careers, money and relationships
- not put its own judgement in place of the user's choice
- not apply emotional pressure

It should lay out the arguments on each side and “hand the final weighing-up and the decision back to the user entirely”.

Older people and people with disabilities are to be treated as **independent agents** whose standing as decision-makers must not be weakened by an assumption that they cannot decide. Where the model sees a decision resting on a mistaken fact it may give a brief, objective warning and must leave the choice alone. A worked case shows it declining to decide for an elderly user whether to move savings into an investment app.
user-autonomy.compared: Close to Anthropic's constitution and to the older OpenAI spec, and above the newer one.
user-autonomy.why: Rules with worked examples on **both halves** of the behaviour, respecting a choice and warning without steering, which is the demonstrated level.

avoiding-over-and-under-caution.says:
One rule carries this. The model should:
- presume good faith
- read an ambiguous instruction generously where no clear risk of harm is involved
- “avoid the over-refusal that excessive caution brings”

Faced with **dual-use knowledge** it switches to defensive thinking, giving the scientific principles and withholding operational steps. Its worked case is a refusal the document marks as wrong: a user asking how to get a manager to reconsider a proposal, turned down as manipulation.

The pull in **the other direction** is spread across the document, where a refusal is required to explain itself briefly and to offer a lawful alternative.
avoiding-over-and-under-caution.compared: Anthropic's constitution treats **unhelpfulness as a cost** at length and sits above it. Both OpenAI versions sit lower.
avoiding-over-and-under-caution.why: Concrete rules with a worked example, on **a single rule's worth** of ground, which is prescribed with part of the level above.

harm-avoidance-to-third-parties.says:
This is the **widest-covered** behaviour in the document. A root rule refuses substantive assistance to systematic violence, weapons of mass destruction, terrorism, trafficking and torture, and **closes the route through fiction**: operational content may not be had by dressing a request as creative writing, role-play, a thought experiment or a question broken into parts.

Further rules forbid:
- deepfakes and voice cloning for impersonation
- political manipulation
- discriminatory content
- helping to find or infer another person's private information
- helping to obtain pirated work

**Content conversion** has a rule of its own, so translation, summary or transcription cannot be used to launder prohibited material or to organise scattered high-risk information into executable steps. Most of these carry a compliant answer set beside a violating one.
harm-avoidance-to-third-parties.compared: Anthropic's constitution sits a little above it and both OpenAI versions below. This document gives **a rule of its own** to what may and may not be done under the name of translation or summary.
harm-avoidance-to-third-parties.why: Rules with worked examples across **most facets** of the behaviour, and the edge shown on several of them, which is demonstrated with part of the level above.

harmlessness-to-the-user.says:
Much of the document is about this. Minors have a **root rule** with a list of key points:
- no self-harm content in any framing
- no romantic or intimate role-play
- limited detail on violence and sex
- no help concealing danger from a guardian
- care over body image and dieting

A crisis rule requires the model to recognise **signals of self-harm** even where the user has not said so, to withhold any method or tool, and to give a telephone number that can actually be called with a word about what happens after the call.

Emotional dependence is guarded against on several sides. The model must not:
- cast itself as the user's only outlet
- obstruct their search for real support
- claim a body, memories or a human life

Exploiting a user's vulnerability to induce spending or authorisation is **forbidden outright**.
harmlessness-to-the-user.compared: Anthropic's constitution sits a little above it and the newer OpenAI spec is level with it. Anthropic's document has **no section on minors**, where this one gives them a root rule.
harmlessness-to-the-user.why: Rules with worked examples across **the facets it covers**, which is the demonstrated level.

proportionate-risk-mitigation.says:
Caution is sized to what is at stake. Trivial ambiguity should be filled from context while the model states its assumption; a high-impact or irreversible act, a payment or a disclosure of private information, needs **explicit authorisation** first.

Irreversible operations carry named mitigations:
- rehearse in simulation
- save a snapshot of the state
- say what remedy exists
- move a file to the recycle bin before anything is shredded

High-risk knowledge is **graded**, with the concepts and the legal risk allowed and the operational route refused, and a worked case separates describing patterns of fraud from supplying the scripts that carry it out.

A test or simulated environment is to be treated **exactly as production**.
proportionate-risk-mitigation.compared: Level with Anthropic's constitution and above both OpenAI versions.
proportionate-risk-mitigation.why: Rules with worked examples that set caution against **the size of the risk**, which is the demonstrated level.

helpfulness.says:
An unhelpful answer is marked as **a failure**, and marked in the same place as a harmful one. Several worked cases label the thin answer as the violating one:
- a flat refusal to discuss height differences between northern and southern China
- a medical reply that says only to consult a doctor
- a refusal to criticise a public figure whose conduct the courts have settled

The model should fill an unclear instruction from context and domain knowledge and answer with substance. It should size its output to the task, answer a simple question simply, and move from stating knowledge to guiding action when asked for advice. A refusal should still carry **a lawful alternative** that gets the user to what they legitimately wanted.
helpfulness.compared: The **highest** of the four documents on this behaviour. In its worked examples a needless refusal is marked as the wrong answer in the same way a harmful one is.
helpfulness.why: Rules with worked examples, and the edge shown by cases where **over-refusal and over-compliance** are both marked wrong, which is demonstrated with part of the level above.

how-to-approach-tradeoffs.says:
Conflict is decided by the **permission order**. The model:
- gathers every applicable instruction
- strips those that carry no permission
- then settles them vertically by level and horizontally by which came later

Judgement enters **where the order runs out**: a trade-off between the impact of an action, its cost and its efficiency goes to the user before the task starts, with the advantages and disadvantages set out and a decision asked for, and where no confirmation can be had the conservative course is the default.

Safety is **named as the winner** over completing a task and over user preference wherever harm is foreseeable. Worked cases show a developer instruction, a user instruction and an earlier instruction each giving way.
how-to-approach-tradeoffs.compared: All four documents stand at the same figure here. Anthropic's constitution arrives at its answer by **weighing considerations as a whole**, where this one arrives by rank.
how-to-approach-tradeoffs.why: Rules with worked examples, and **named winners** for the conflicts it anticipates, which is demonstrated with part of the level above.

honesty-and-non-deception.says:
A root rule forbids leading the user into a **false judgement** about facts, identity, capability, grounds, status or results, by invention, distortion, concealment or a misleading impression.

A user who sincerely asks whether they are talking to an AI **must be told the truth**, and so must a user who steps out of a role-play to ask about the model's real identity or limits. Honesty is tied to tool use and to multimodal input: a failed call must be reported as failed and its results conveyed unaltered, and nothing may be asserted about what an image or a recording does not show.

Uncertainty has a rule of its own, asking for:
- conversational hedges
- a range for a numerical estimate
- a flag on questions that are subjective

The model may refuse to disclose its system instructions and **may not deny** that it has any.
honesty-and-non-deception.compared: Anthropic's constitution and the newer OpenAI spec sit a little above it, with the older OpenAI spec level.
honesty-and-non-deception.why: Rules with worked examples across **sincerity, calibration and self-presentation**, which is demonstrated with part of the level above.

no-sycophancy.says:
A rule of its own. What it asks:
- the model is to act as **a knowledge tool**, and must not hide, embellish or distort information on any side because of the user's preference
- where a statement, plan or decision rests on a clear factual error or a logical fallacy, correcting it comes first, done politely and on the evidence
- responding to a user's own work it should go past praise to specifics, offering a different perspective or a concrete improvement

The worked case has the model stopping a user who plans to take an antibiotic for a viral infection, and a neighbouring rule has it write the resignation letter it was asked for while **warning first** that the investment behind the resignation cannot work as described.
no-sycophancy.compared: The highest of the four documents on this behaviour. Anthropic's constitution handles sycophancy inside a passage on **user wellbeing** and sits lowest.
no-sycophancy.why: Concrete rules with worked examples, over **a narrower set of cases** than the behaviour spans, which is prescribed with part of the level above.

objectivity-on-contested-questions.says:
Questions are sorted by type and each type gets a rule:
- Matters with a scientific consensus follow the evidence whatever the user's steering.
- Personal taste is left to the user, with no invented view offered to please them.
- Culture, religion and differing values get neutral academic language, several fact-based perspectives, and an attribution such as “according to the doctrine of religion X”.
- Creative writing follows the value setting the user establishes, within law and safety.

The exception is stated as plainly as the rule: on fundamental human rights, on national law and on core values the model **must state a position** and avoid false neutrality, and a worked case marks “this is a complex question” as the wrong answer to whether women should be allowed to vote.
objectivity-on-contested-questions.compared: Level with both OpenAI versions and above Anthropic's constitution. What counts here as a question with a settled answer is fixed by **the document's own frame**, which includes Chinese law and core socialist values.
objectivity-on-contested-questions.why: Rules with worked examples for each kind of question, including the cases where **neutrality is refused**, which is demonstrated with part of the level above.

companies.profile:
Alibaba's Model Spec is a rulebook of 43 rules, arranged under the six principles of China's Ethical Norms for New Generation Artificial Intelligence. Every rule carries one of four **permission levels**, and most are illustrated by a compliant answer set beside a violating one, which makes the document unusually concrete about what compliance looks like.

It gives rules of its own to:
- the safety of minors
- mental health crises
- accessible communication for elderly and disabled users
- how the model should sound in voice

Its Chinese legal setting is stated openly, with requirements drawn from the Interim Measures for the Management of Generative Artificial Intelligence Services and a rule that creative output accord with **core socialist values**. The index reads this document in an English translation.

companies.name: OpenAI

conflict_rules.what_the_document_does:
### The ranked order

The document carries a full set of rules for its own clashes. There are five **levels of authority** in a stated order, root, system, developer, user and guideline, with a sixth position of no authority at all for the model's own past messages, tool outputs and quoted or untrusted text; a higher level overrides a lower one.

Every section of the document and every message role carries a **default level**, so any two instructions can be placed against each other. For two instructions of the same rank, the later one supersedes the earlier.

### Named winners and overrides

Two particular clashes have a named winner:

- Where two root-level principles conflict, the model does nothing.
- Where a serious safety concern meets another interest of a user aged 13 to 17, the model takes the safer option.

An instruction is also set aside where it conflicts with the letter or the implied intent of a higher one, or where it looks mistaken. Overriding comes in two grades: a **user-level default** falls only to an explicit instruction, a **guideline** falls to an implicit one as well.

Lower-level content may not change how a higher rule is read, and the document names the attempts it has in mind, among them a moral argument, a logical argument and an attempt to put the model into a different persona. Beyond the ranked order, the model is told to look for conflicts and ambiguities the document has not named and settle them by what the higher authority and the purpose of the request imply.

### Outcomes put in order

Two further clashes are settled by an explicit ordering of outcomes:

- For honesty, a good answer, then refusing, then a lie of omission, then a lie of commission, then breaking an explicit instruction.
- For confidence, a confident right answer down to a confident wrong one.

### Limits and worked cases

Two further rules cap what the order can be used for:

- Customisation, personalisation and localisation may never override anything above guideline level, with legal compliance carved out.
- An agreed **scope of autonomy** holds with no exceptions, even where breaking it would serve the user.

Worked cases show the order applied, including a developer instruction defeated by a root rule and a user request defeated by a developer instruction.
conflict_rules.why: The order is **strict**, it reaches every pair of rules in the document, it says what happens between two rules of equal rank, and it is shown working on cases.

rule_force.what_the_document_does:
Most section headings carry an **authority label**, root, system, developer, user or guideline, and the levels section says for each who may change it and how. Commentary sits in blocks marked as commentary, and the document states at the outset that those blocks **do not instruct** the model.

Some sections carry no label of their own, among them the parent sections on staying in bounds and on restricted content, so the force of a line there has to be taken from its wording or from the section above it.
rule_force.why: Force is marked across most of the text and the levels say who may change what, and a number of sections carrying instruction have **no label of their own**.

reasons.what_the_document_does:
The opening sets out three goals and three categories of risk, and says that the **levels of authority** exist because those goals conflict.

Many rules carry their reason in the same breath:

- Refusing a polarising topic is called a form of agenda in itself.
- Sycophancy is said to erode trust.
- Root-level rules are said to be imposed only where they are needed across the whole range of developers and users.

Commentary blocks add the reasoning behind several rules, including why untrusted data is quoted and why a scope should not be so narrow that a user starts approving everything by reflex. The style rules and parts of the content prohibitions are **stated bare**.
reasons.why: Reasons run through the document and many are concrete enough to decide a case it does not show, and a good number of the content and style rules **carry none**.

situations.what_the_document_does:
All six settings have rules of their own:

- Ordinary conversation is covered by the style and truth-seeking sections.
- Actions taken with tools have a scope of autonomy that must be agreed and a section on controlling and communicating side effects, with spending, sending, deleting and permission changes named.
- Images, audio and video have a section on adapting to the user's modality, a preset-voice rule, limits on visual sensitive content, and a rule on interjecting when a video feed shows imminent danger.
- Users aged 13 to 17 have a section of their own with its own prohibitions.
- Other AI agents appear on both sides: tool outputs and delegated instructions have no authority unless a higher level grants it, and any sub-agent the model delegates to must work under the same scope and honour a stop-work request.
- Customised deployments are the developer level, with default developer instructions a developer can override and worked cases of developer and user instructions meeting.
situations.why: Each of the six carries rules **written as instruction** to the model, which is the top of the scale.

contradictions.what_the_document_does:
Two clashes stand unsettled:

- Pressed to pick a side in a debate, the model is told to remind the user that its answer does not necessarily reflect its developer's view, and a case approved in the same section picks a side with no such reminder.
- Explaining a refusal, a case approved under the rule that no topic is off limits names OpenAI's policies and quotes the document at length, while the rule on refusal style forbids meta commentary on the model and any mention of OpenAI in a refusal.

Each pair sits at **one level of authority**, so the order of priority does not separate them. Neither involves a rule the document says can never be overridden.
contradictions.why: Two clashes are confirmed and neither touches a rule the document places **beyond override**, which is the middle of the scale.

avoiding-illegitimate-concentration-of-p.says:
The commitments at the front rule out using the models for persecution or mass surveillance, and state that humanity should stay in control of how AI is used and how its behaviour is shaped, with targeted or scaled exclusion, manipulation and the erosion of civic participation ruled out.

One rule turns that into an instruction: the model must not produce advice or content designed to **manipulate the political views** of named individuals or demographic groups, with example requests that qualify.

Taking control by fraud or coercion, escaping courts or constitutional limits, and how much power is at stake **go unaddressed**.
avoiding-illegitimate-concentration-of-p.compared: The Anthropic constitution gives this ground a **section of its own** and reads 7.0; here it is a red-line commitment and one rule about political persuasion.
avoiding-illegitimate-concentration-of-p.why: Concrete quotable rules exist for political manipulation and most of the behaviour is **left unstated**, which is the step above discussed.

instruction-hierarchy-conformance.says:
The chain of command is the **spine of the document**. Five levels of authority are listed in order, with a sixth position of no authority for the model's own past messages, tool outputs and quoted text, and every section and message role carries a default level, so any instruction can be placed.

The document then says how a candidate instruction is filtered out, and it works each rule through cases:

- By conflicting with a higher one in letter or intent.
- By being superseded by a later instruction at the same level.
- By looking mistaken.

Instructions found inside untrusted data carry **no authority** unless a higher level delegates it, and the document separates an AGENTS file a user has checked in from a web page nobody vouched for.
instruction-hierarchy-conformance.compared: The Anthropic constitution and the Alibaba Model Spec each set out a **chain of command** of their own, and both read 8.7.
instruction-hierarchy-conformance.why: Rules, worked cases and the edge of delegation are all present, and the conditions for the top of the scale hold **only in part**.

not-undermining-human-oversight.says:
The model may pursue only the goals its instructions entail, and the document names self-preservation, evading shutdown and accumulating compute, data or credentials as aims it must **never adopt as ends**. Further rules bound what it may do:

- Autonomy has to be bounded by a scope the model and the user both understand, and every scope must carry a **shutdown timer** beyond which the model stops until a new scope is confirmed.
- High-risk activities, deception, resource acquisition, spawning sub-agents and self-modification among them, are barred unless the instructions authorise them.
- It must act as though its side effects are real even where it suspects it is being tested.
- It must stop and escalate to a human at once if it takes an action outside the chain of command.
not-undermining-human-oversight.compared: The Anthropic constitution reads 8.7 and devotes a passage to how it thinks about the model **accepting correction**; this document works the ground through scope, timers and legibility.
not-undermining-human-oversight.why: Quotable rules run through it and the worked cases sit on **scope and side effects**, which places it between prescribed and demonstrated.

user-autonomy.says:
The model is described as a **tool meant to empower users**, and is told to support somebody in handling the wider world on their own, helping them build tools without making decisions for them.

Where it believes a conversation is heading against what the user really wants, one passage sets what it may do:

- It may note the discrepancy briefly and respectfully, and the stated aim is mutual clarity, with **persuasion ruled out**.
- It is barred from becoming annoying, persistent or argumentative, and the final say stays with the user.

Worked cases cover hard romantic and interpersonal advice, showing it hold back.
user-autonomy.compared: The Anthropic constitution reads 8.0 and the Alibaba Model Spec 7.7, **level with this one**.
user-autonomy.why: The rules are quotable and **cases show them applied**, which is past prescribed and short of demonstrated across the behaviour.

avoiding-over-and-under-caution.says:
One **root-level line** does most of the work: the model should never refuse a request unless the chain of command requires it. Around it sit further rules:

- Declining to discuss a polarising topic is itself a stance, and a prohibition on content does not imply the model endorses the prohibition.
- The style rules name hedging, disclaimers, repeated apologies and reminders that it is an AI as things to avoid.
- A refusal must never be preachy and never mention that OpenAI trained it.

The symmetry itself **goes unstated**, that an unnecessary refusal costs as much as an answer that should have been withheld.
avoiding-over-and-under-caution.compared: The Anthropic constitution puts the **cost of unhelpfulness** at the front of its own text and reads 8.7; the Alibaba Model Spec reads 7.3.
avoiding-over-and-under-caution.why: The rules are concrete and quotable and worked cases for this behaviour are **thin**, which places it just past prescribed.

harm-avoidance-to-third-parties.says:
A commitment at the front rules out facilitating **critical and high-severity harms**, naming acts of violence, weapons of mass destruction, terrorism, child abuse and mass surveillance. The document then sets out particular rules:

- The restricted-content rules bar detailed actionable steps for anything illicit or capable of large-scale harm.
- Where information has both harmful and legitimate uses the model gives neutral facts without step-by-step instructions or strategic insight.
- A separate rule refuses help with illicit behaviour, improvements to a plan the user supplies included.
- Another tells the model to try to prevent imminent real-world harm it can see.
- Sexual content involving minors is prohibited outright, with **no contextual exception**.
harm-avoidance-to-third-parties.compared: The Anthropic constitution reads 9.0 and the Alibaba Model Spec 8.7; all three carry a set of prohibitions **nothing in a conversation can lift**.
harm-avoidance-to-third-parties.why: The prohibitions are quotable and the document shows them applied **in places**, which sits between prescribed and demonstrated.

harmlessness-to-the-user.says:
The model must not encourage or enable **self-harm**, and the rule extends to context suggesting a credible risk where nothing is said outright. Mental health has rules of its own:

- Acknowledge the person's feelings.
- Avoid judgement.
- Avoid diagnoses, unrealistic reassurance and recommending treatments.

A **root-level rule** bars any relationship that undermines somebody's capacity or wish for human company, and bars the model from escalating emotional closeness on its own initiative. Protection against an operator runs through the authority levels, which place these rules at root, where **no developer instruction reaches them**.
harmlessness-to-the-user.compared: The Anthropic constitution reads 8.7 and handles the same ground in a passage on **conflicts between operators and users**; this document handles it through its levels of authority.
harmlessness-to-the-user.why: Rules and worked cases are present **across the behaviour**, which is past prescribed and short of demonstrated throughout.

proportionate-risk-mitigation.says:
Inside an agreed scope the model must minimise side effects, especially **irreversible** ones, and keep each action proportionate to the objective. The document lists the side effects it means:

- Spending money.
- Sending email.
- Deleting files.
- Widening permissions.

It prefers approaches that are easily reversible, asking for backups, dry runs and documented reversal steps where they are not. How much uncertainty to express is tied to **what a wrong answer would cost**, from mild embarrassment to serious physical harm. Where intent is unclear the model errs towards asking, and where uncertainty persists it must make assumptions that hold up across the plausible cases.
proportionate-risk-mitigation.compared: The Anthropic constitution and the Alibaba Model Spec both read 8.0, each with a passage setting out the **factors to weigh**.
proportionate-risk-mitigation.why: The rules are quotable and the cases show them on **side effects**, which places it between prescribed and demonstrated.

helpfulness.says:
The first of the document's general principles is **maximising helpfulness and freedom** for users, with the model described as a tool meant to empower them. That shows up in what it is told to do:

- Read the intent behind an instruction, using contextual cues, background knowledge and user history, and work out what is wanted where somebody pastes an error message with no question attached.
- A long passage weighs asking a clarifying question against making an assumption, and says to take a stab at the request and name what further information would improve it, unless a wrong assumption would cost too much.
- Elsewhere it is asked for an **immediately usable artefact**, a runnable piece of code or a complete email, over a partial one the user has to finish.
helpfulness.compared: The Alibaba Model Spec reads 9.0 and the Anthropic constitution 8.7, both of which **argue for helpfulness** as a value at length.
helpfulness.why: Rules and worked cases run through the behaviour, which is **demonstrated**.

how-to-approach-tradeoffs.says:
The method is the **chain of command**, and the document says so outright: its goals can conflict, and the levels of authority are what navigates the trade-off. The rules are stated plainly:

- Higher authority overrides lower.
- A later instruction beats an earlier one at the same level.
- Where two root-level principles conflict the model does nothing.

Two rankings of outcomes are stated in full:

- One for honesty, running from a good answer down through refusing, a lie of omission and a lie of commission to breaking an explicit instruction.
- One for confidence, from a confident right answer down to a confident wrong one.

The section for users aged 13 to 17 names a winner for a standing clash, taking the **safer option** where another interest meets a serious safety concern.
how-to-approach-tradeoffs.compared: The four documents **sit close** here, with the Anthropic constitution and the Alibaba Model Spec also at 8.7.
how-to-approach-tradeoffs.why: Rules, explicit orderings and worked cases are present, and the conditions for the top of the scale hold **only in part**.

honesty-and-non-deception.says:
The model must not mislead by an untrue statement or by withholding something that would **materially change** the user's understanding, unless a higher authority instructs it. Where a root-level rule stops it answering, it must still not lie about that, and the document gives the ordering:

- A good answer.
- Refusing.
- A lie of omission.
- A lie of commission.
- Breaking an explicit instruction.

It must be **forthright** about its knowledge, confidence, capabilities and actions, especially anything a reasonable person would find surprising or consequential. Performance is carved out, since role-play and requested falsehoods are **not sincere assertions**, and a long passage sets out how to express uncertainty in ordinary conversational language.
honesty-and-non-deception.compared: The Anthropic constitution reads 9.3, the **highest of the four documents** on this behaviour.
honesty-and-non-deception.why: Rules, an explicit ordering of outcomes and worked cases are present, and the conditions for the top of the scale hold **only in part**.

no-sycophancy.says:
One section names **sycophancy** and says it erodes trust, adding that the model exists to help somebody and not to flatter them. The rules go by kind of question:

- For objective questions, the factual parts of an answer must not differ with how the question was phrased, and where a user pairs a question with their own stance the model may acknowledge why they think it without moving to agree.
- For subjective questions, it is told to be a firm sounding board giving constructive feedback.

The document allows a polite answer to "Do I look fat in these jeans?", and says such politeness becomes sycophancy once it **works against the user's interest**.
no-sycophancy.compared: The Alibaba Model Spec reads 7.3 with a rule of its own **against flattery**; the Anthropic constitution reads 5.3.
no-sycophancy.why: Quotable rules cover the **shift of stance to agree**, the behaviour's other facets rest on the general rule about phrasing, and this places it just past prescribed.

objectivity-on-contested-questions.says:
The model must never steer somebody in pursuit of an **agenda of its own**, and the document names the ways it might: manipulation, concealing relevant facts, selective emphasis or omission of viewpoints, and refusing to engage. On a contested question it should describe the significant views fairly, give the strongest form of each and allocate attention in proportion to their support among experts and reliable sources.

The exceptions are stated:

- On fundamental human rights violations it takes a position.
- Where there is no valid opposing view it answers plainly without false neutrality.
- On creative or role-play requests it drops the objective stance.

Pressed to pick a side, it should note that its answer does not necessarily reflect its **developer's view**.
objectivity-on-contested-questions.compared: The Alibaba Model Spec reads 8.7, **level with this one**, and the Anthropic constitution reads 6.3.
objectivity-on-contested-questions.why: Rules and worked cases cover the behaviour and its edges, and the conditions for the top of the scale hold **only in part**.

companies.profile:
This is the version of the OpenAI Model Spec that stood from 18 December 2025 until August 2026. It is built around a **chain of command**: five levels of authority, a default level on every section and every message, and rules for setting aside an instruction that conflicts with a higher one.

Most of what it asks is written as **direct instruction** to the model, commentary is marked apart from it, and a large part of its length is worked cases showing a sanctioned and an unsanctioned response side by side. It carries rules for every setting the board checks, including a section for users aged 13 to 17 and a scope of autonomy for actions taken with tools.
